title: Nvidia earnings and Anthropic's IPO headline a heavy week ahead
dek: US markets are closed for the weekend after a mixed Friday in which chip stocks fell again on the Nvidia leadership crisis while the S&P 500 still logged a 2.5% weekly gain. Next week brings Nvidia's first report without Jensen Huang, Anthropic's planned Nasdaq debut, retail sales and the Fed's October minutes, with the 10-year yield above 5%.
quick: Weekend edition: no trading today. On Friday the S&P 500 fell 0.4%, the Nasdaq 0.9%, and the Dow rose 0.1%; the S&P still gained 2.5% for the week.
Nvidia closed lower again and posted its sixth straight weekly decline; AMD, Broadcom and Intel fell harder. Nvidia reports Tuesday after the close.
October producer prices rose 0.3%, a bit below the 0.4% forecast, but the annual rate of 6.5% is the highest since late 2022.
The 10-year Treasury yield ended near 5.14%, and futures still price a December Fed hike as close to certain, mostly a quarter point.
Anthropic plans to price its IPO Wednesday and begin trading on Nasdaq Thursday, in what banks are pitching as one of the largest listings ever.
Gold fell about 4% on the week to near 13-month lows, Bitcoin slid to about $67,000, and the yen sits just under 160 per dollar.

blocks.head: Nvidia's leadership crisis keeps weighing on chip stocks
blocks.what: Jensen Huang resigned as Nvidia's CEO on Thursday after scrutiny of an affair with a woman reported to be a Chinese intelligence asset and a relationship with a subordinate; finance chief Colette Kress is interim CEO. Nvidia opened higher Friday but closed down about 2%, near $163, and has now fallen six weeks in a row, its longest weekly losing streak since 2012, according to CNBC and MarketWatch. The selling spread Friday: AMD closed down roughly 9% after an intraday drop near 11%, and Broadcom and Intel also fell sharply, reversing gains made Thursday on bets that rivals would win business from Nvidia.
blocks.why: Nvidia and the chipmakers are among the largest weights in the S&P 500 and Nasdaq, so their swings move the indexes. The tech sector ETF fell 2% Friday, and investors are reassessing how much of the AI spending boom depended on Huang's dealmaking.
blocks.watch: Nvidia's earnings Tuesday after the close, its first without Huang, and any word on a permanent successor.

blocks.head: Wholesale inflation cooled a little in October but stays high
blocks.what: The producer price index rose 0.3% in October, slightly under the 0.4% economists expected, after a 1.3% jump in September. Over the past year, producer prices are up 6.5%, the biggest annual gain since November 2022. Core producer prices, excluding food and energy, rose 0.3% for the month, in line with forecasts, and about 5% from a year earlier. Earlier in the week, consumer prices rose 0.4% in October versus a 0.3% forecast.
blocks.why: Two hot inflation reports in one week have pushed Treasury yields higher and cemented bets on a Fed rate hike in December, which pressures richly valued growth stocks and non-yielding assets like gold and Bitcoin.
blocks.watch: Whether consumer spending holds up in Tuesday's retail sales report despite higher prices.

blocks.head: Fed officials line up behind more rate hikes
blocks.what: Boston Fed President Susan Collins said Friday that some additional tightening is appropriate soon and that a firmer path than she expected a few months ago may be needed, while declining to say how high or how fast. Philadelphia Fed President Anna Paulson said earlier in the week that further gradual hikes look appropriate, and Chicago Fed President Austan Goolsbee called the October consumer price report borderline disturbing. The Fed's policy range is 3.75% to 4.00%; the next meeting is December 8 to 9.
blocks.why: A hiking Fed raises borrowing costs across the economy and keeps upward pressure on bond yields, the dollar and mortgage rates, while weighing on rate-sensitive stocks such as small caps and homebuilders.
blocks.watch: Chair Kevin Warsh's remarks Monday and the October meeting minutes Wednesday.

blocks.head: Anthropic's IPO is set for next week
blocks.what: Anthropic has said it expects to price its initial public offering on or about Wednesday and begin trading on Nasdaq under the ticker ANT on Thursday. The indicated range is $70 to $78 per share for about 825 million shares. The Wall Street Journal reported the company is targeting a valuation of roughly $1.33 trillion or more, and the New York Times said banks are pitching it as potentially the largest public offering ever.
blocks.why: A deal this large can draw money from other holdings as investors make room, a point MarketWatch raised about crypto. Its reception will also be read as a test of investor appetite for AI after the Nvidia shock.
blocks.watch: The final price Wednesday night and whether the range is raised beforehand.

blocks.head: Outages hit air travel and Microsoft services
blocks.what: The FAA halted departures nationwide Friday afternoon, its longest ground stop since 9/11 according to the BBC, before lifting it after more than four hours; officials blamed a telecommunications outage and the Homeland Security secretary said there was no evidence of a cyberattack. Cancellations are expected to stretch into the weekend. Separately, Microsoft said Outlook, Teams and other 365 services were fully restored after a disruption lasting more than a day.
blocks.why: Airline stocks may react Monday to the cost of cancellations and rebookings, which MarketWatch noted could be harder with airlines flying fewer flights because of high fuel costs.
blocks.watch: Airline updates on cancellation counts and any cause found for the FAA outage.

blocks.head: Washington fallout from the Nvidia case
blocks.what: Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent faulted the Commerce Department for not putting Singapore-based Megaspeed on the export blacklist, as scrutiny grows over AI chip sales reaching China. Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick faces questions about his family's business ties to Nvidia, CNBC and the BBC reported. US officials told CNBC that President Trump does not plan to raise the Nvidia matter on his upcoming China trip, where he is set to meet China's Xi and Russia's Putin.
blocks.why: Tighter export controls would affect chipmakers' China revenue; Nvidia's current guidance already assumes no China data center sales.
blocks.watch: Any new entity-list actions from Commerce.

blocks.text: Asia

Asian markets were mixed Friday. Japan's Nikkei 225 rose about 0.5% to 61,142, while Hong Kong's Hang Seng fell about 1.6% and Shanghai slipped 0.6% as AI-linked shares in the region came under pressure from the Nvidia news. Asian markets reopen Sunday evening US time; China's monthly activity data and the Reserve Bank of Australia's minutes are on next week's schedule.
Europe

Europe's Stoxx 600 closed essentially flat at 664.14, a record high, and gained about 2.4% for the week, its best week since early summer. Insurers and oil companies offset weakness in chipmakers. London's FTSE 100 rose 0.4% to 10,903, its highest close in three months, and Germany's DAX was little changed. UK inflation and jobs data are due next week.
Currencies

The dollar index ended near 103.4, close to a 19-month high, and had its biggest weekly gain since September, according to Reuters, as Fed hike bets grew. The yen is at about 159.7 per dollar. Japan's finance minister said the government will respond appropriately to volatility after the yen briefly touched 160 Thursday; Tokyo spent 15.4 trillion yen supporting the currency after it hit nearly 164 in late July. The euro is about $1.102, the pound about $1.322, and the yuan about 6.67 per dollar, all little changed on the day.

US markets are closed today. On Friday the S&P 500 fell 0.4% to 7,561.67 and the Nasdaq Composite fell 0.9%, while the Dow edged up 0.1% to 52,347.55, the only major index higher. The Russell 2000 slipped 0.3% and the VIX volatility gauge rose to about 19.3. Stocks opened higher and faded as chip selling resumed and the 10-year yield moved back above 5%.

For the week the picture was better: the S&P 500 gained 2.5%, its first winning week since early October, as stocks recovered from the sharp AI selloff of November 5, when the index fell 4.4%. Futures resume trading Sunday evening; Nvidia's report Tuesday is the biggest scheduled single-stock risk of the week.

The 10-year Treasury yield rose about 4 basis points Friday to roughly 5.14%, after trading as high as 5.17% during the day. The 30-year yield climbed to about 5.47%, while the 2-year dipped about 1 basis point to near 4.85%. That leaves the 10-year roughly 29 basis points above the 2-year, a steeper curve that reflects investors demanding more to hold long-term debt as inflation stays high.

Fed funds futures, tracked by CME Group's FedWatch tool, price a December hike as nearly certain: about 89% odds of a quarter-point move and the rest on a half point. Governor Christopher Waller has raised the possibility of a half-point move, and markets also lean toward another increase in January, according to Reuters. Collins, Paulson and Goolsbee all pointed to the need for more tightening this week, though they differ on pace.
Fed speakers next week (confirmed so far)

items: Monday: Fed Chair Kevin Warsh, about noon ET.
Wednesday: Minutes of the October meeting, when the Fed held rates steady; they were written before the hot October inflation reports.
Thursday: Chicago's Austan Goolsbee, Richmond's Tom Barkin, Governor Michael Barr and Philadelphia's Anna Paulson.

blocks.text: Technology was by far the weakest S&P 500 sector Friday, with the sector ETF down about 2%, as chip stocks sold off. Consumer discretionary, industrials and materials also slipped modestly. The leaders were defensive and value groups: consumer staples rose about 1.4%, communication services about 1.1%, energy about 1%, and financials about 0.8%, with health care and utilities each up around 0.5%. The pattern fit a week in which money rotated out of AI names and toward steadier businesses.
Names to watch Monday

items: Nvidia: down about 13% from its November 6 close; investors are positioning ahead of Tuesday's results and guidance.
AMD, Broadcom, Intel: Friday's drop erased Thursday's gains as the 'rivals benefit' trade unwound.
Airlines: exposed to the cost of Friday's nationwide ground stop and weekend cancellations.
Microsoft: services restored after a global outage; watch for any customer credits or fallout.
Retailers: Home Depot, Lowe's, Target and Walmart report this week, giving a read on holiday-season spending.

blocks.text: Oil

Oil ended a second straight weekly decline. Brent settled near $95.84 a barrel, little changed Friday, and US crude ended just under $89, down about 2.5% for the week. The International Energy Agency now expects a supply surplus in the fourth quarter, about 1.7 million barrels a day more than demand, the first since the Iran war began in February. Prices are well below their October peak, but shipping risks in the Middle East persist, and MarketWatch noted diesel prices remain far above prewar levels.
Gold

Gold settled near $3,888 an ounce, down about 4% to 4.5% for the week depending on the measure and near its lowest level in about 13 months. Higher Treasury yields and a stronger dollar raise the cost of holding a metal that pays no interest.
Crypto

Bitcoin is trading around $67,200, down about 2.4% over the past day and roughly $7,000 lower than a week ago, with Ether near $1,900. US spot Bitcoin ETFs saw about $1.07 billion of outflows from November 9 to 13, after $1.28 billion the prior week, according to Farside data, and BlackRock's fund has seen outflows for 11 straight sessions. Rising rate-hike bets and forced selling of leveraged positions have added pressure.
There are no US economic releases, Fed speakers or market sessions today or Sunday. The next scheduled items arrive Monday:

items: Monday 8:30 a.m. ET: New York Fed's Empire State manufacturing survey for November; the prior reading was 25.5.
Monday about noon ET: Fed Chair Kevin Warsh speaks; any comment on the size of a December hike would move rates.

Tuesday 8:30 a.m. ET: October retail sales; economists polled by Newsquawk expect a 0.2% gain after 0.8% in September, with the 'control group' seen up 0.4%. Industrial production follows the same morning.

blocks.text: No major companies report this weekend. These are next week's key reports, by date as listed in company calendars and previews from Morningstar, Kiplinger and Newsquawk.

rows: Analysts expect about $3.84 a share on $42.8 billion in revenue; housing demand with mortgage rates above 7%.
Consensus near $108.8 billion revenue and $2.47 a share vs. company guidance of $108 billion; next-quarter outlook and comments from interim CEO Colette Kress.
Home improvement spending and its full-year outlook.
Discretionary spending trends and holiday-quarter guidance.
Analysts expect about 63 cents a share on $187.2 billion revenue; a BofA analyst expects a possible raised full-year outlook.

blocks.text: This is a dense week for the AI trade, inflation and the Fed. Monday brings the Empire State survey and Fed Chair Warsh. Tuesday is the biggest day: October retail sales and industrial production in the morning, Home Depot before the open, and Nvidia after the close, where investors will focus on whether revenue beats the $108 billion guidance and what the company forecasts without Huang. Wednesday has the Fed's October minutes, Target and Lowe's, and Anthropic's expected IPO pricing. Thursday brings Anthropic's first trade on Nasdaq, Walmart's results and four Fed speakers. Overseas, UK inflation and jobs reports and China's activity data are due. With the 10-year near 5.14% and a December hike largely priced in, hotter-than-expected spending data or hawkish comments from Warsh would test that pricing, while a strong Nvidia report could steady chip stocks.

bottom_line: Markets head into the weekend with a weekly gain for the S&P 500 but fresh pressure on chipmakers, yields above 5% and a December Fed hike largely priced in. Next week's Nvidia results, Anthropic IPO and retail sales are the main scheduled tests.
